tldr: By combining a diffusion policy trained purely in simulation with an adaptive controller that corrects contact forces and position errors in real time, researchers achieved zero-shot transfer on real hardware for high-precision timber joinery, pipe fitting, and full-scale truss assembly—without collecting any real-world data.
hero_caption: Overview of the proposed framework. Trajectories with force/torque and position data are automatically generated in simulation to train a diffusion policy. During real-world deployment, an L1-inspired adaptive controller cancels out contact disturbances online to achieve zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.
overview:
The construction industry faces worsening labor shortages and heavy physical demands, creating high demand for robotic automation. However, contact-rich tasks with clearances below 1 mm—such as timber joinery (mortise and tenon) or pipe fitting—easily fail due to jamming caused by fabrication tolerances and uncertain contact friction, especially when robots simply follow pre-planned trajectories.

While popular imitation learning methods like diffusion policies can produce compliant motions, collecting hundreds of trial-and-error demonstrations on real robots handling heavy, construction-scale materials is impractical. The risks of workpiece wear, breakage, and hardware damage are too high. To address this, the team came up with a smart strategy: handle all data collection and training inside a physics simulator (Isaac Sim), and use a real-time adaptive controller to compensate on the fly for contact modeling errors during sim-to-real transfer.

In this approach, the diffusion policy is pre-trained on automatically generated simulation trajectories containing noisy position and force/torque profiles. At execution time, an online correction loop inspired by $\mathcal{L}_1$ adaptive control—widely used in aerospace engineering—estimates deviations caused by unmodeled contact forces and material friction, slightly tweaking the policy's commands in real time.

In real-robot evaluations, the framework achieved a 100% success rate on single-task assemblies: timber joinery (1 mm clearance) and PVC pipe fitting (0.25 mm clearance). Furthermore, it achieved 90–100% success across a 3-step sequential contact-rich insertion process to assemble a full-scale timber gable truss (span ~2.8 m). It also kept contact forces significantly lower than baseline methods, ensuring safe assembly.
contributions: Built a scalable data generation pipeline that synthesizes large amounts of position and force/torque trajectories in simulation, training construction assembly diffusion policies without hazardous, expensive real-world demonstrations.
Proposed a novel hybrid control architecture based on $\mathcal{L}_1$ adaptive control theory that modulates adaptive gains based on contact forces to correct policy predictions online.
Achieved complete zero-shot sim-to-real transfer of simulation-trained policies, reaching 100% success on single tasks and 90–100% success on sequential full-scale truss assembly.

Conducted rigorous non-parametric statistical tests on peak contact forces beyond simple success rates, demonstrating that the proposed method significantly reduces excessive forces and lowers wear on both workpieces and the robot.

sections.heading: Can we solve tight-clearance construction contacts using only simulation?
sections.summary: Automating construction tasks is essential to boost productivity and reduce physical strain, but tight-tolerance assembly remains notoriously hard due to fabrication errors and uncertain contact dynamics. This paper introduces a framework that pairs simulation-trained diffusion policies with $\mathcal{L}_1$-inspired adaptive control, achieving zero-shot transfer without any real-world demonstrations.
sections.details:
Robotic automation in construction holds great potential for solving skilled labor shortages and relieving workers from strenuous tasks. However, building assemblies such as walls, floors, and structural frames frequently involve contact-rich manipulation with clearances of just a few millimeters or less. Conventional pre-planned trajectory approaches often suffer from jamming due to workpiece fabrication inaccuracies, tolerance stack-ups, and unmodeled friction, easily leading to task failure or material damage.

Policy learning methods using force and position feedback, such as diffusion policies, have drawn substantial attention. Yet collecting hundreds of real-robot demonstration trials on construction-scale hardware is unrealistic due to component wear, machine fatigue, and workplace safety hazards. Simulation-based data collection is an appealing alternative, but a large sim-to-real gap persists between rigid-body simulation contact models and real-world dynamics.

This is the core insight of the study: train the policy solely in simulation, and let a fast, $\mathcal{L}_1$-inspired adaptive controller cancel out unmodeled real-world disturbances—such as unexpected contact dynamics, friction, and workpiece compliance—online. This two-tier design enables zero-shot transfer without requiring any real-world trial and error.

sections.heading: Bringing together construction robotics, model-based control, and policy learning
sections.summary: The paper contextualizes its approach across three research lineages: construction site assembly, classic hybrid position/force and impedance control, and modern learning-based control including diffusion policies. The proposed work bridges existing limitations by blending learning-based trajectory generation with model-based adaptive disturbance compensation.
sections.details:
Related work can be categorized into four primary areas:

- Construction robotic assembly: Early pick-and-place approaches for bricklaying or timber framing mostly relied on simple butt joints that tolerate positioning errors. Tight assemblies like mortise-and-tenon joints require online force feedback adjustments, but gathering real-world demonstrations is prohibitively expensive.

- Model-based contact control: Classical hybrid position/force control and impedance control require precise manual specification and tuning of contact constraints, task frames, and stiffness parameters. They struggle to adapt to piece-to-piece variations.

- Learning-based control: While reinforcement learning and imitation learning with domain randomization have progressed, inaccurate contact models in simulators have made zero-shot transfer of tight-clearance assemblies difficult. Furthermore, most prior diffusion policy studies have been confined to tabletop setups with loose geometric constraints.

- Combining learning with model-based control: Recent works pair admittance or variable impedance control with learned policies. Building on this direction, this paper incorporates $\mathcal{L}_1$ adaptive control theory developed in aerospace applications, delivering robust disturbance rejection capable of handling heavy-load, contact-rich construction assembly.

sections.heading: Synthetic data pipeline and $\mathcal{L}_1$-inspired adaptive controller design
sections.summary: Diffusion policies are trained on parallel synthetic trajectories with force and position data in Isaac Sim. On the real robot, an $\mathcal{L}_1$-inspired state predictor, adaptation law, and control law estimate disturbances in real time to correct policy outputs. An adaptive scaling mechanism engages primarily under high contact forces to keep interactions safe.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Experimental Platform
The physical hardware consists of a 6-axis UR20 arm with a 20 kg payload, a wrist-mounted 6-axis force/torque (F/T) sensor, and a custom pneumatic parallel gripper. NVIDIA Isaac Sim 5.0 serves as the simulation environment, faithfully reproducing nominal geometries and material properties while collecting data rapidly across parallel GPU instances.

### 3.2 Synthetic Data Collection
The assembly task is split into two phases: approach above the target and insertion. Initial poses receive random horizontal offsets (radius $r_{samp}=5\,\mathrm{mm}$) and vertical offsets (approach height $z_{app}=60\,\mathrm{mm}$ with variance $z_{\max}=20\,\mathrm{mm}$). In addition, low-frequency perturbations (up to 2 mm amplitude) are injected into the insertion path to deliberately cause contact interactions. Only trajectories that successfully reach within 2 mm of the target without exceeding 1000 N of contact force are kept, downsampled to 10 Hz, and added to the dataset.

### 3.3 Diffusion Policy Training
A CNN-based diffusion policy is trained to take histories of end-effector positions $\bm{p}\in\mathbb{R}^3$ and 6-axis forces/torques $\bm{\mathcal{F}}\in\mathbb{R}^6$ over an observation horizon $T_o$, and predict future relative displacements $\bm{u}_{pol}\in\mathbb{R}^3$ over a horizon $T_p$. To maintain high replanning frequency, only the first $T_a$ steps of the predicted chunk are executed.

### 3.4 $\mathcal{L}_1$-Inspired Adaptive Controller
Because unmodeled contact disturbances $\bm{\sigma}(t)$ cause the robot to deviate from policy predictions, an adaptive control loop with three components is implemented (Figure F5):
- State Predictor: Predicts the next state $\hat{\bm{p}}(t)$ from nominal system dynamics and estimated disturbances. For safety, it resets if the tracking error exceeds 50 mm.
- Adaptation Law: Updates estimated disturbances $\hat{\bm{\sigma}}(t)$ using the prediction error $\bm{e}(t)=\hat{\bm{p}}(t)-\bm{p}(t)$. A sigmoid activation function $\alpha(t)$ keyed to contact force magnitude $\|\bm{F}(t)\|$ suppresses adaptation during free motion and fully activates it during contact. Estimates are stabilized with projection operators and a 10 Hz low-pass filter.
- Control Law: A force-dependent scaling factor $\beta(t) = 1/(1+k_d \|\bm{F}(t)\|)$ smoothly slows down policy velocity commands under high contact forces (adding compliance), while subtracting the filtered disturbance $-\hat{\bm{\sigma}}_{filtered}(t)$ to form the final command $\bm{u}_{cmd}$.

captions.F5: Block diagram of the adaptive controller. The diffusion policy command $\bm{u}_{pol}$ is force-scaled, and the estimated contact disturbance $\hat{\bm{\sigma}}_{filtered}$ from the state predictor and adaptation law is subtracted to generate safe, disturbance-compensated commands $\bm{u}_{cmd}$.
captions.F3: Initial pose sampling during data generation. (a) Horizontal offset sampling within a 5 mm radius disk around the target. (b) Vertical trajectory profile and dispersion showing the transition from the 60 mm approach height down to the 0 mm target depth.

sections.heading: Benchmarking single tasks and scaling up to full-scale truss assembly
sections.summary: The approach was benchmarked against baselines and compliant control across two single-insertion tasks with distinct materials and geometries (timber joinery and PVC pipe fitting). It was then evaluated on a full-scale sequential assembly of a 4-member timber gable truss.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Single-Task Assembly Setup
Two assembly benchmarks were tested (Figures F6, F7):
- Timber joinery (mortise and tenon): Rectangular insertion with 1 mm clearance on opposing sides. Characterized by high rigidity, high friction, and risk of excessive force.
- PVC pipe fitting: Cylindrical insertion with a tight 0.25 mm radial clearance. Although clearance is extremely small, the material has slight structural compliance.

Models were trained on 1,000 simulated trajectories per task and evaluated across three controller modes:
- Baseline: Directly executes diffusion policy predictions.
- Ours: Diffusion policy outputs corrected online by the proposed adaptive controller.
- Compliant policy: A benchmark combining the policy with a compliant controller from prior work.

Performance metrics included success rate (reaching within 3 mm of the target depth) and peak contact force ($F_{\max}$) per trial. Because peak contact forces follow non-normal distributions, they were evaluated using non-parametric Kruskal-Wallis and Mann-Whitney U tests (with Bonferroni corrections) alongside effect sizes (CLES and Cohen's $d$).

### 4.2 Full-Scale Truss Assembly Experiment
To test real-world scalability, a robotic workcell assembled a full-scale timber gable truss with a span of roughly 2.8 m, comprising four members: a tie beam, a king post, and left and right rafters (Figure F8). With the tie beam clamped in place, the UR20 robot sequentially inserted the king post, left rafter, and right rafter. After king post insertion, a second collaborative industrial robot held the post to stabilize it for subsequent rafter insertions, mimicking real construction procedures. Given the large mass and dimensions of the members, the force threshold was raised to 300 N.

captions.F7: Comparison between simulation (top) and real-world setups (bottom). Left column shows timber joinery, right column shows PVC pipe fitting. Simulation only models nominal geometry; real-world friction and flex are absorbed by the adaptive controller.
captions.F8: Overall view of the full-scale gable truss (left) and exploded view of components (right). The tie beam features mortises at its center and both ends, joining the vertical king post via a mortise-and-tenon joint, and the rafters via angled tenons and an apex lap joint.

sections.heading: 100% success, drastically lower contact forces, and material differences
sections.summary: The proposed method achieved 100% success on real-world single tasks and 90–100% across full-scale truss assembly subtasks. While it substantially reduced peak contact forces in rigid timber, all methods succeeded on compliant PVC pipes, highlighting the strong influence of material properties on contact control.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Single Assembly Results
The proposed framework demonstrated clear superiority in success rates across both simulation and real hardware (Table 5).
- In timber joinery, where the baseline suffered from jamming or force limit exceedances on the real robot, our method scored a 100% success rate. The compliant policy reached 95%, but force analysis (Table 6) revealed a stark contrast: our method yielded significantly lower peak forces than the compliant policy ($p_{corr}<0.001$, CLES $=0.93$, Cohen's $d=1.60$), ensuring smooth, tightly regulated insertions.
- In PVC pipe fitting, all methods reached 100% success on real hardware. PVC's low friction and minor elastic deformation allowed the pipe to self-align and absorb misalignments despite the tight 0.25 mm clearance. This shows that adaptive disturbance compensation is most critical when handling rigid materials like timber.

### 5.2 Full-Scale Truss Assembly Results
In sequential real-robot truss assembly, success rates reached 100% for the king post, 100% for the right rafter, and 90% for the left rafter (Table 7). Despite substantial contact forces and moments generated by handling large components, the independently trained diffusion policies and adaptive controller cooperated seamlessly, producing a stable, self-supporting timber gable truss. This validates that sequentially invoking separate policies can successfully scale to complex, multi-stage physical structures.

sections.heading: Takeaway and future outlook: Paving the way for contact-rich construction robotics
sections.summary: This work successfully demonstrates zero-shot contact-rich assembly without real-world demonstrations by uniting simulation-trained diffusion policies with an $\mathcal{L}_1$-inspired adaptive controller. Future directions include vision integration, automated controller tuning, and multi-axis complex joinery.
sections.details:
The primary contribution of this paper is showing that contact-rich, high-precision assembly can transfer zero-shot without any real-world demonstrations when diffusion policies are combined with a fast adaptive control loop. Detailed statistical analyses of peak contact forces also proved that the adaptive controller serves as an effective safeguard, preventing robot wear and component breakage.

Several hurdles remain before deployment on job sites. The current framework assumes target locations are provided accurately in advance, without online vision-based perception. Furthermore, adaptive controller hyperparameters (such as $k_d$ and filter bandwidths) were hand-tuned in simulation, requiring manual effort for new tasks. Looking ahead, integrating vision-language-action (VLA) models, automating gain tuning via meta-learning or reinforcement learning, and handling 3D angled insertions will further expand the framework across broader construction workflows.

takeaways: Dividing labor between simulation-trained diffusion policies for coarse trajectory planning and model-based ($\mathcal{L}_1$-inspired) adaptive control for real-time contact disturbance rejection represents a powerful sim-to-real transfer paradigm.
Evaluating contact-rich tasks requires looking beyond simple success rates to the statistical distribution of peak contact forces, which is vital for preventing component and machine wear.

Rigid, high-friction materials like timber benefit most from adaptive disturbance compensation, whereas compliant materials like PVC can self-align via elastic deformation, requiring material-aware control strategies.
Sequentially executing independently simulation-trained policies makes it possible to scale up to complex multi-step construction processes, such as assembling full-scale structural trusses.
limitations: Lacks vision-based object perception, assuming nominal coordinates and target locations of mating parts are accurately known ahead of time.
Hyperparameters of the adaptive controller (such as gains and filter cutoff frequencies) rely on manual tuning in simulation, requiring engineering effort for each new assembly.
Focuses purely on translational insertions with fixed end-effector orientations, and does not yet handle multi-axis 3D insertions requiring angled wiggling or twisting motions.
